newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban sets conditions for ceasefire talks.
newsitem.headline: Taleban sets conditions for ceasefire talks.

text.p: The radical Islamic Taleban movement said on Sunday it would take part in talks on a ceasefire in Afghanistan's factional warfare on condition no action was taken against its administration or Islamic law.
"We have conditions for negotiations and a ceasefire," the acting information minister in the Taleban administration, Amir Khan Mutaqi, told journalists in Kabul.
"Nobody should do anything against the establishment of the Islamic government which is already in place or oppose the implementation of sharia (Islamic law).
"If these points are accepted, we are ready for any kind of negotiations."
He also rejected an opposition demand that the capital should be demilitarised.

The head of the U.N. Special Mission to Afghanistan, Dr. Norbert Holl, has been shuttling between the warring factions in an attempt to get them to sit down together to find a peaceful solution to the fighting.

The acting foreign minister in the Taleban administration met a representative of northern Afghan leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum in Pakistan last month for what the United Nations described as "technical-level discussions".
The United Nations said the meeting was amicable but that no firm conclusions were reached.
The United Nations proposes that three representatives of the Taleban should meet three representatives of the opposition.
The opposition is made up of three main factions loyal to the ousted government, to General Dostum and to Shi'ite Moslem leader Karim Khalili.
The United Nations says Dostum and the former government's military commander, Ahmed Shah Masood, have signalled their willingness to participate in talks.
Mutaqi said the Taleban had always been in favour of a peaceful solution to the conflict.
"From the first days of our establishment we have been pressing for a peaceful solution, and I hope that others will follow this lead," he said.
However, Mutaqi rejected an opposition call for Kabul should be demilitarised.
"The opposition demand for the demilitarisation of Kabul is an irrational issue," he said.
"It is irrational because Kabul is already run by a police force. If anyone insists on this matter, it means they want further looting of Kabul.
"For the first time in 17 years Kabul is peaceful and we will not accept any deal which insists on the demilitarisation of the city."
